title: Krishnamoorthi Breaks With Indian-American Democrats on Russia Sanctions Vote
excerpt: The Illinois Democrat was the sole Indian-origin House member to back the Graham sanctions bill carrying 100% tariff authority on Russian oil buyers including India.
body:
• Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi was the only Indian-American member of the US House to vote for the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning of Russia and Iran Act, which passed 262-159.
  • The other five Indian-American Democrats — Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera, Shri Thanedar and Suhas Subramanyam — voted against the bill.
  • The legislation would authorize tariffs of up to 100% on the top buyers of Russian oil and gas, a group that includes India and China.
  • Krishnamoorthi's vote came days after he met Illinois Ukraine Action and affirmed US support for Ukraine; he is retiring from the House in January after losing the Illinois Senate primary.

Raja Krishnamoorthi has split from every other Indian-American Democrat in the House. The Illinois congressman voted in favour of a sweeping Russia sanctions bill this week, emerging as the lone Indian-origin "yes" among the six Indian-American members of the chamber.

The House passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning of Russia and Iran Act on Wednesday by 262 votes to 159, sending it to President Donald Trump, who plans to sign it into law. The bill targets Russia's energy and defence industries and its "shadow fleet" of tankers, and it would give the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas — a list that includes India and China.

A rare break in the bloc

All six Indian-American members of the House are Democrats, which made the division notable. Krishnamoorthi's five colleagues — Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera, Shri Thanedar and Suhas Subramanyam — voted no. Fifty-eight Democrats overall supported the measure, joining all but seven Republicans.

The bill also extends sanctions on Iran and, notably, carves out an exemption for US purchases of uranium from Russia.

Krishnamoorthi's position was shaped by Ukraine advocacy. Days before the vote he met with Illinois Ukraine Action, a Ukrainian advocacy group, and posted on X that Ukrainians were continuing to fight for their freedom and sovereignty and that the United States should maintain its support.

The India question

The vote is uncomfortable precisely because of the constituency it implicates. An amendment sponsored by Democrat Steny Hoyer named India among ten countries initially eligible for duties of up to 100% over purchases of Russian crude oil and natural gas, along with China, Türkiye, the UAE and others. The provision does not automatically impose tariffs; it places the named countries in the category for which the president could impose additional duties.

New Delhi has defended its Russian energy purchases as part of its energy-security strategy and says it follows applicable sanctions. India has been a major buyer of discounted Russian crude since the invasion of Ukraine began, making it one of the countries most exposed if Trump uses the authority.

Krishnamoorthi himself has been one of the most prominent voices on India-US ties in Congress — he previously pushed back at a "go home" jibe with the line "I'm staying, so is the curry." His yes vote puts him on the other side of a measure that could directly raise costs for Indian refiners.

A final-session vote

The timing matters. Krishnamoorthi lost the Democratic primary for the US Senate in March and is scheduled to retire from the House in January, freeing him from the usual electoral arithmetic. The bill, nearly a year and a half after the late Senator Lindsey Graham first introduced it, is the most significant Ukraine-related legislation Congress has passed since Trump returned to the White House.

Whether the tariff authority is used — and how hard it lands on India — now sits with the White House. For the Indian-American community that has watched its House delegation vote as a bloc for years, the split is the story: one of their own broke ranks on the bill that could tax India's oil.
